Permeability from Stokes flow ​

Before this page

Extension to conductivity, whose Darcy row is the starting point here, and Concentration and contribution tensors for the tensors that the schemes combine.

In the dictionary of Extension to conductivity, Darcy's law makes the permeability a conductivity. That reading holds when every phase is itself a porous medium of known permeability (Darcy–Darcy upscaling). It does not hold at the scale of the pores, where the fluid obeys the Stokes equations and the solid admits no flow at all. Bignonnet (2022) showed that the estimates of continuum micromechanics nonetheless carry over to this Stokes-to-Darcy upscaling. Their auxiliary problem is no longer Eshelby's but a Brinkman inhomogeneity problem, whose solution depends on the size of the inclusion. This page states that formulation in the notation of the package. The syntax is given in Brinkman inclusions, and the estimates are compared in the application Stokes-to-Darcy permeability of porous media.

1. Two scales of flow ​

At the scale of the material, the filtration velocity and the pressure of a fluid of viscosity obey Darcy's law,

At the scale of the pores, a representative volume holds a fluid domain and a rigid solid . The pressure gradient   acts as a uniform load on the Stokes flow in the pores, with no slip on the solid and periodic fluctuations:

The problem is linear in , so      with a velocity concentration field , set to zero in the solid. Averaging the velocity then yields the permeability,  .

2. Extension to the solid ​

Elasticity splits a volume average over the phases. To do the same here, the Stokes problem is extended to the whole of by a body force exerted on a fictitious fluid occupying the solid. The force vanishes in the true fluid, keeps the velocity zero in the solid, and its average balances the pressure gradient,  . Under a prescribed average velocity , the velocity and the force are linear in :

For any uniform tensor , the homogenized resistance then splits over regions of volume fractions :

This is the counterpart of the decomposition of the effective stiffness on which every scheme rests. What remains is to estimate each regional average from an auxiliary problem.

3. The Brinkman inhomogeneity problem ​

The auxiliary problem places one pattern of region in an unbounded reference medium of permeability   . In the reference medium and in a porous inclusion of permeability , the body force is Brinkman's drag (Brinkman, 1949):

with   far from the inclusion. A clear fluid is the limit   (Stokes flow), and a solid the limit   (no flow, and an undetermined force whose resultant is the traction on the solid). Following Bignonnet (2022), the viscosity is the same in every medium, and the velocity and the traction   are continuous across every interface. Both assumptions are restrictions, since an effective viscosity and a stress jump at a clear-fluid–porous interface have been proposed, but neither comes with a predictive value.

The averages over the inclusion define the velocity concentration and the average drag per unit :

and their combination is the resistance contribution tensor

symmetric by the reciprocity of the Brinkman problem. With the velocity in the role of the gradient and the drag density in that of the flux, these are exactly the gradient-side concentration, the flux-side concentration and the contribution tensor that the schemes consume. The package therefore enters Brinkman inhomogeneities through the level B of the custom-inclusion interface.

Why the size enters. Brinkman's equation compares the viscous term with the drag : they balance over the screening length  . An inclusion of size is therefore characterized by   (and   inside a porous one). The problem is not invariant under a change of scale, so its solution is not a property of the shape alone and there is no Hill tensor. As   the viscous boundary layers become thin and Darcy's law is recovered, together with the conduction inclusion problem.

Two formulations. Under a prescribed remote force instead of a velocity, the force concentration (  ) and the average velocity   play the same roles in terms of permeability, and the two descriptions are related pointwise by    . The resistance form is finite for a clear-fluid reference ( ) and the permeability form for an impervious one ( ). In the permeability form the gradient-side quantity is the force density, which derives from a potential far from the inclusion, as the gradient of conduction does. Its Darcy limit is therefore exactly the conduction inclusion problem with as conductivity. This is the form in which the Hill tensor of conduction may be used, as Maxwell's scheme requires.

4. The sphere ​

The derivation below is the one carried out symbolically in scripts/71_brinkman_permeability.jl with the curvilinear operators of TensND, along the approach of The elastic sphere, solved symbolically (operators: Curvilinear differential calculus).

5. The schemes ​

With the contribution tensors of the patterns evaluated in the appropriate reference, the schemes read as in conduction:

where labels the matrix, the current fraction of inclusions and their filling rates. The differential scheme with impervious spheres in a clear fluid is the iterated dilute approximation of Wilkinson (1985). Maxwell's scheme requires the contribution of an equivalent inclusion of the shape of the distribution. For an ellipsoid much larger than the screening length, that contribution is the Darcy one, given by the Hill tensor of conduction in the permeability form.

Three consequences hold whatever the microstructure. First, a scheme built on a clear-fluid matrix (dilute, Mori–Tanaka) captures only the leading term of the drag on a sparse bed. The self-consistent scheme, whose reference is the porous effective medium itself, reproduces the correction in predicted for random beds of spheres (Howells, 1974; Hinch, 1977; Kim and Russel, 1985). Second, the drag on an impervious cylinder vanishes in a clear fluid (Stokes' paradox): no dilute, Mori–Tanaka or differential estimate exists for fibers in a fluid matrix. Third, the self-consistent scheme percolates at a threshold set by the shapes chosen for the pores,   for spherical grains and pores, and it does not percolate at all with cylindrical pores.

6. Numerical evaluation ​

Each formulation evaluates its closed forms in its own variable:   in the resistance form and    in the permeability form. Each is a rational function that stays finite at its own end of the range. The porous closed forms subtract nearly equal terms as  , and read at  . They are rewritten with

which tend to , , , and . For   these are summed from the Taylor series of and of . The coefficients follow from the Riccati equations    and     that the two functions satisfy. A nearly fluid porous inclusion therefore keeps full accuracy, as the tests check against 256-bit evaluations of the published closed forms.

Where to go next ​

The next chapter changes the time dependence rather than the physics: The Laplace-Carson approach reduces a non-aging viscoelastic problem to an elastic one.
